title: Buildings are a high-emissions economic system whose transition depends on affordability, codes, materials, and investment
source_unit: UNEP and Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction, Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2025-2026
geography: Global buildings and construction sector, including construction, renovation, demolition, engineering, building operations, policy, technology, and investment

observations.period: 2025-2026; global buildings and construction economic and environmental footprint

denominator.unit: global buildings and construction sector frame

gdp_share.unit: percent of global GDP represented by buildings and construction

workforce_share.unit: percent of the world's workforce employed across construction, renovation, demolition, and engineering

co2_share.unit: percent of global CO2 emissions attributed to the sector

material_extraction_share.unit: nearly percent of global material extraction associated with buildings and construction

observations.method: UNEP and GlobalABC global sector assessment of economic activity, employment, emissions, and material extraction.
observations.uncertainty: Sector boundaries, accounting methods, and the distinction between construction activity, building operations, and embodied materials affect the reported shares.
observations.subgroup: Construction and engineering workers, building owners and occupants, material producers, cities, investors, regulators, and communities exposed to building costs and environmental burdens.
observations.counterinterpretation: A large sector footprint also creates leverage: efficiency, material substitution, electrification, and better design can produce broad environmental and economic gains.

observations.period: 2025-2050; building stock growth and long-lived lock-in

denominator.unit: global buildings existing or expected by 2050

future_stock.unit: percent of buildings that will exist in 2050 still to be built or renovated

transition_window.value: current construction and renovation choices shape emissions, energy use, resilience, and quality of life for generations

policy_route.value: align new construction, renovation, codes, materials, and building operations with a 2050 net-zero pathway

observations.method: UNEP and GlobalABC assessment of future building stock, long-lived infrastructure, and transition pathways.
observations.uncertainty: The future-stock estimate is a global planning approximation and does not specify where construction, renovation, or climate exposure will occur.
observations.subgroup: Future occupants, renters and owners, construction firms, local governments, utilities, material suppliers, and communities planning urban growth.
observations.counterinterpretation: Retrofit, adaptive reuse, compact development, and stronger standards can reduce lock-in; future stock is not predetermined by current construction patterns.

observations.period: 2015-2025; building energy intensity and green certification

energy_intensity_change.unit: percent change in global building energy intensity

green_certifications.unit: change in green building certifications over the last decade

transition_signal.value: performance and certification are improving, but progress remains insufficient for the 2050 pathway

affordability_link.value: climate action in buildings must also deliver resilience and affordable living

observations.method: UNEP and GlobalABC tracking of building energy intensity, certification, policy, technology, and investment against a net-zero pathway.
observations.uncertainty: Global averages conceal variation by climate, building type, energy mix, code enforcement, income, and certification quality.
observations.subgroup: Building occupants, landlords, tenants, builders, energy providers, certifiers, and communities affected by bills, indoor conditions, and climate risk.
observations.counterinterpretation: Certification growth may reflect market adoption and does not alone establish realized energy savings, lower bills, or equitable access to efficient buildings.

required_investment.unit: trillion US dollars of energy-efficiency investment needed by 2030

investment_direction.value: investment must more than double to keep climate goals within reach

implementation_system.value: finance, codes, technology, workforce capability, and policy coordination must move together

distributional_question.value: the transition must connect efficiency investment with affordable living and resilience rather than only premium construction

observations.method: UNEP and GlobalABC pathway assessment of policy, technology, and investment requirements for building energy efficiency.
observations.uncertainty: The investment figure is a pathway requirement, not a guaranteed financing commitment or a forecast of realized spending; costs vary by region and building stock.
observations.subgroup: Public and private investors, households and tenants, construction workers, cities, utilities, developers, and communities facing retrofit and housing-cost decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Innovation, falling technology costs, stronger standards, public finance, and demand reduction could change the required investment mix and timing.

related_sources.claim: UNEP's prior Buildings-GSR editions provide the historical sector-tracking series.
GlobalABC provides complementary buildings-sector policy and implementation materials.

boundary: This record adds a built-environment route across emissions, materials, jobs, building stock, energy performance, affordability, resilience, codes, and investment. It uses aggregate global sector analysis, not respondent-level housing histories, individual utility bills, property records, building inspections, causal forecasts, or proof that every city or household follows the same pathway.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNEP publication page reviewed for sector GDP, workforce, emissions, material extraction, future building stock, energy intensity, green certification, affordable living, and investment findings.
